L000018	\title{Transverse thermophotovoltaics from nonreciprocal plasmon drag in metal}
L000019	
L000020	\author{Dingwei He}

L000029	\begin{abstract}
L000030	Transverse thermophotovoltaics has been conceptually proposed as a paradigm distinct
L000031	from conventional junction-based photovoltaics, but has so far lacked a theoretical
L000032	foundation. In this Letter, we establish a microscopic formalism of this effect in which a
L000033	transverse electric current emerges in a two-dimensional metal sheet via nonreciprocal
L000034	surface plasmon polaritons driven by near-field thermal radiation. This theoretical
L000035	formalism incorporates the electron-photon interaction by integrating electronic
L000036	transition factor governed by energy-momentum conservation, the photon flux factor
L000037	encoding the nonreciprocal surface modes, and their directional coupling.  Our approach
L000038	quantitatively confirms the plasmon-drag mechanism and reveals the role of impurity
L000039	scattering. This work provides a rigorous theoretical foundation for transverse
L000040	thermophotovoltaic devices and opens avenues for active nanoscale thermal energy
L000041	conversion.
L000042	\end{abstract}
L000043	
L000044	\maketitle
L000045	
L000046	{\it Introduction.}
L000047	
L000048	
L000049	
L000050	
L000051	Transverse thermophotovoltaics, the generation of an electric current perpendicular to a
L000052	thermal gradient across two radiating objects, offers a paradigm distinct from
L000053	conventional junction-based photovoltaics.
L000054	Recent work by Tang et al. proposed a near-field transverse thermoelectric effect by
L000055	harnessing the nonreciprocity of surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs) in a system composed of
L000056	graphene and magneto-optic medium~\cite{GT21}. In that model, the nonreciprocal dispersion
L000057	of the surface waves produces an asymmetric momentum transfer to electrons in graphene for
L000058	counterpropagating modes. This results in a directional electric current, controlled by an
L000059	external magnetic field, which emerges transversely to the thermal gradient.
L000060	This effect fundamentally differs from traditional near-field thermophotovoltaics, which
L000061	relies on semiconductor p-n junctions to generate a longitudinal (parallel to the thermal
L000062	gradient) electric current~\cite{TPV06, TPV-review18, TPV-review21-1, TPV-review21-2,
L000063	TPV-review23}. While this work proposed a conceptual framework, a microscopic description
L000064	has been lacking.
L000065	
L000066	To establish a rigorous theoretical foundation for this effect, we develop in this Letter
L000067	a microscopic formalism based on the nonequilibrium Green's function
L000068	technique~\cite{Henne08, JSW23, JSW25, Haug_Jauho}. It allows us to treat the
L000069	electron-photon interaction in a fully quantum-mechanical manner, essential for capturing
L000070	the interplay between momentum-conserving electronic transitions, nonreciprocal plasmon
L000071	dispersion, and their directional coupling through near-field radiative transfer.  A
L000072	physically transparent expression for the transverse current is obtained through a
L000073	leading-order expansion of the electron-photon interaction and electron damping. Our
L000074	theory not only confirms the earlier prediction quantitatively but also elucidates the
L000075	influence of impurity scattering that were inaccessible in previous phenomenological
L000076	descriptions. Furthermore, we propose several practical strategies to enhance the
L000077	transverse current.
L000078	
L000079	\begin{figure}
L000080	\centering
L000081	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig1.pdf} \\
L000082	\caption{(a) Schematic of the transverse thermophotovoltaic effect in a system consisting
L000083	  of a semi-infinite magneto-optic medium and a two-dimensional metal sheet at different
L000084	  temperatures, separated by a vacuum gap $d$. A magnetic field $B$ along the
L000085	  $y$ direction applied to the magneto-optic medium generates nonreciprocal surface
L000086	  plasmon polaritons (SPPs) that propagate along the $x$ direction. For a positive
L000087	  $y$-directed field, the SPP branches propagating in the $+x$ direction and $-x$
L000088	  direction are red- and blue-shifted, respectively. This spectral asymmetry creates a net
L000089	  photon-momentum transfer to electrons in the metal sheet, resulting in a transverse
L000090	  electric current powered by near-field thermal radiation.
L000091	  (b) Nonreciprocal electronic transition in a single-layer graphene with linear
L000092	  dispersion by absorption of a near-field photon with large in-plane momentum
L000093	  $\hbar\bm{q}$. The photon transfers energy $\hbar\omega$ and momentum $\hbar\bm{q}$ to
L000094	  an electron, scattering it from state $|\bm{k}\rangle$ to $|\bm{k}+\bm{q}\rangle$. Since
L000095	  the incident photon flux originates from the nonreciprocal SPPs, the transition
L000096	  probability differs for $+q_x$ and $-q_x$. This imbalance yields a net momentum transfer
L000097	  along the $x$-direction, underlying the generation of the transverse current shown in
L000098	  panel (a). }
L000099	\label{fig1}
L000100	\end{figure}
L000101	
L000102	{\it Theoretical formalism.}
L000103	We model the transverse thermophotovoltaic effect in a system comprising a semi-infinite
L000104	magneto-optic medium which fills the space of $z<0$ and a two-dimensional metal sheet
L000105	separated by a vacuum gap of distance $d$, as sketched in Fig.~\ref{fig1}(a).
L000106	The metal sheet and the magneto-optic medium are at different temperatures, $T_1$ and
L000107	$T_2$, respectively.
L000108	The magneto-optic medium, taken to be InSb, is subjected to an external magnetic field
L000109	along the $y$ direction. Its dielectric response at frequency $\omega$ is described by the
L000110	gyrotropic tensor~\cite{InSb_76}
L000111	\begin{equation} \label{epsilon_MO}
L000112	  \epsilon_{\rm MO}(\omega) =
L000113	  \begin{bmatrix}
L000114	    \epsilon_d & 0 & i\epsilon_a \\
L000115	    0 & \epsilon_p & 0 \\
L000116	    -i\epsilon_a & 0 & \epsilon_d
L000117	  \end{bmatrix} .
L000118	\end{equation}
L000119	
L000120	
L000121	This gyrotropy breaks time-reversal symmetry and supports nonreciprocal SPPs that
L000122	propagate along the $x$ direction.
L000123	An alternative route to nonreciprocity exploits materials with intrinsic magneto-optical
L000124	activity, such as magnetic Weyl semimetals. These systems host nonreciprocal surface
L000125	polaritons without an external field, owing to their inherent anomalous Hall
L000126	conductivity~\cite{WSM_SPP16, Kotov18, WSM_AHE_20nc, GT_WSM}.
L000127	
L000128	The total Hamiltonian is decomposed as $H_{\rm tot} = H_{\rm ph} + H_1 + H_{1, {\rm ph}}$.
L000129	The electromagnetic environment, including the magneto-optic medium and the free space, is
L000130	described by $H_{\rm ph}$. The metal sheet is described by the electronic Hamiltonian
L000131	$H_1$ and its coupling to the electromagnetic field by $H_{1, {\rm ph}}$. The electric
L000132	current induced by nonreciprocal plasmon drag is computed within the nonequilibrium
L000133	Green's function formalism~\cite{Haug_Jauho}.
L000134	We neglect Zeeman splitting induced by the magnetic field, and the spin and
L000135	valley degeneracies are incorporated by an overall factor of $4$ in the electric current
L000136	expression. Expanding to the second order in the electron-photon interaction strength and
L000137	to the first order in electron damping parameter $\eta$ in the metal, the steady state
L000138	electric current along $x$ direction is expressed as [see End Matter for details]
L000139	\begin{equation} \label{Ie}
L000140	  I_e = -\frac{4 e_0}{\eta} \int d X \ \Delta_x(\bm{k},\bm{q}) L(\bm{k}, \bm{q}, \omega)
L000141	  M(\bm{k}, \bm{q}, \omega) N_{21}(\omega) ,
L000142	\end{equation}
L000143	where $e_0$ is the elementary charge and the integration measure is
L000144	\begin{equation*}
L000145	  \int dX = \int \frac{d^2\bm{k}}{(2\pi)^2} \int_{q>\omega/c}
L000146	  \frac{d^2\bm{q}}{(2\pi)^2} \int_0^\infty \frac{d\omega}{2\pi} .
L000147	\end{equation*}
L000148	The integration runs over the electron wavevector $\bm{k}$, the in-plane photon wavevector
L000149	$\bm{q}\equiv (q_x, q_y)$, and photon frequency $\omega$.
L000150	The restriction $q \equiv |\bm{q}|>\omega / c$ with $c$ the speed of light focuses the
L000151	discussion on the near-field region, where evanescent waves dominate.
L000152	The velocity difference $\bm{\Delta}(\bm{k},\bm{q}) = \bm{v}(\bm{k} + \bm{q})
L000153	- \bm{v}(\bm{k})$
L000154	with $\bm{v}(\bm{k})$ the electron group velocity enters as an electron scatter from
L000155	state $|\bm{k}\rangle$ to state $|\bm{k} + \bm{q}\rangle$ by absorbing a photon of
L000156	momentum $\hbar\bm{q}$.
L000157	The electronic transition factor
L000158	\begin{equation} \label{L}
L000159	  L(\bm{k},\bm{q}, \omega) = {\rm Im} \left[ \frac{f(\varepsilon_{\bm{k}}-i
L000160	  \eta)-f(\varepsilon_{\bm{k}+\bm{q}}+i \eta)}{\hbar\omega +
L000161	  \varepsilon_{\bm{k}}-\varepsilon_{\bm{k}+\bm{q}} -2i \eta} \right] ,
L000162	\end{equation}
L000163	where $\varepsilon_{\bm{k}}$ is the electronic dispersion, and
L000164	\begin{equation} \label{Fermi-Dirac}
L000165	  f(E) = \frac{1}{\exp[(E-\mu)/(k_B T_1)]+1}
L000166	\end{equation}
L000167	is the Fermi-Dirac distribution with chemical potential $\mu$, gives the energy- and
L000168	momentum-resolved transition probability density for photon absorption.
L000169	The denominator of $L$ ensures that the transition is most likely when the photon energy
L000170	$\hbar\omega$ matches the energy difference between the final electronic state $|\bm{k} +
L000171	\bm{q}\rangle$ and the initial one $|\bm{k} \rangle$ [See Fig.~\ref{fig1}(b)].
L000172	
L000173	Since the electronic transition factor depends on the band dispersion, which also dictates
L000174	the electron group velocity, a microscopic framework beyond the conventional fluctuational
L000175	electrodynamics is essential for modeling the electric-current generation.
L000176	The photon interaction strength
L000177	\begin{equation} \label{M}
L000178	  M(\bm{k},\bm{q}, \omega) = \frac{e_0^2 \hbar |\gamma_0|}{\epsilon_0 \omega^2}
L000179	  \Phi(\bm{q}, \omega) \big[ \bm{v}(\bm{k},\bm{q}) \cdot \hat{\bm{q}} \big]^2 ,
L000180	\end{equation}
L000181	with $\epsilon_0$ the vacuum permittivity and $\gamma_0 = \sqrt{(\omega/c)^2-q^2}$ the
L000182	out-of-plane decay constant, quantifies the coupling between the evanescent
L000183	electromagnetic field and the electrons in the metal.
L000184	The symmetrized velocity is given by $\bm{v}(\bm{k},\bm{q}) = [ \bm{v}(\bm{k})
L000185	+ \bm{v}(\bm{k} + \bm{q})] /
L000186	2$.
L000187	The photon flux factor
L000188	\begin{equation}
L000189	  \Phi(\bm{q}, \omega) = \frac{{\rm Im}\big( r_2^p \big) |t_1^p|^2 e^{-2 |\gamma_0|
L000190	  d}}{|1 - r_1^p r_2^p e^{-2 |\gamma_0| d}|^2}
L000191	\end{equation}
L000192	describes the evanescent wave that reaches the metal sheet.
L000193	Here $r_2^p$ is the Fresnel reflection coefficient for $p$-polarization waves incident from
L000194	vacuum onto the magneto-optic interface, which is the source of the nonreciprocity. Its
L000195	calculation detail is provided in the Supporting Information of Ref.~\cite{GT_WSM}.
L000196	The reflection and transmission coefficients at the vacuum-metal interface are determined
L000197	by the sheet conductivity $\sigma(\omega)$:
L000198	\begin{equation} \label{r1p}
L000199	  r^p_1(q, \omega) = 1- t^p_1(q, \omega)
L000200	  = \frac{\gamma_0\sigma( \omega)}{2\epsilon_0\omega + \gamma_0\sigma( \omega)} .
L000201	\end{equation}
L000202	The directional factor $\bm{v}(\bm{k},\bm{q}) \cdot \hat{\bm{q}}$ reflects
L000203	that only the component of the electron velocity parallel to the photon momentum
L000204	$\hat{\bm{q}}$ couples to the $p$-polarized electric field. In our geometry,
L000205	nonreciprocity occurs along the $x$ axis, and this selection rule ensures that the induced
L000206	electric current flows in the same direction. The thermodynamic drive for the current
L000207	generation is provided by the Bose–Einstein distribution difference between the two
L000208	bodies:
L000209	\begin{equation} \label{N21}
L000210	  N_{21}(\omega) = \frac{1}{\exp(\hbar\omega/k_B T_2)-1} -
L000211	  \frac{1}{\exp(\hbar\omega/k_B T_1)-1} .
L000212	\end{equation}
L000213	The sign of $N_{21}(\omega)$ determines the direction of the heat flux and hence the
L000214	momentum transferred to the electrons. Consequently, reversing the temperature gradient
L000215	reverses the current direction.
L000216	
L000217	
L000218	{\it Numerical results.}
L000219	For the numerical calculations,
L000220	the components of the dielectric tensor in Eq.~\eqref{epsilon_MO} are given by
L000221	\begin{align*}
L000222	  \epsilon_d &= \epsilon_{\infty} \left\{ 1+ \frac{\omega_L^2 -\omega_T^2}{\omega_T^2
L000223	  -\omega^2 -i\Gamma\omega} + \frac{\omega_p^2(\omega+i\gamma)}{\omega\big[
L000224	\omega_c^2-(\omega+i\gamma)^2 \big]} \right\}, \\
L000225	  \epsilon_p &= \epsilon_{\infty} \left[ 1+ \frac{\omega_L^2 -\omega_T^2}{\omega_T^2
L000226	  -\omega^2 -i\Gamma\omega} - \frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega(\omega+i\gamma)} \right], \\
L000227	  \epsilon_a &= \frac{\epsilon_{\infty}\omega_p^2\omega_c}{\omega\big[ (\omega+i\gamma)^2
L000228	  -\omega_c^2 \big]} .
L000229	\end{align*}
L000230	The parameters of InSb are taken from Ref.~\cite{InSb_76} with
L000231	the high-frequency dielectric constant $\epsilon_\infty = 15.7$,
L000232	the longitudinal optical phonon frequency $\omega_L = 3.62\times 10^{13}\,{\rm rad/s}$,
L000233	the transverse optical phonon frequency $\omega_T = 3.39\times 10^{13}\,{\rm rad/s}$,
L000234	the phonon damping constant $\Gamma = 5.65\times 10^{11}\,{\rm rad/s}$,
L000235	the free-carrier damping constant $\gamma = 3.39\times 10^{12}\,{\rm rad/s}$,
L000236	the plasma frequency $\omega_p = 3.14\times 10^{13}\,{\rm rad/s}$, and
L000237	the cyclotron frequency $\omega_c = 8.02\times 10^{12}\,{\rm rad/s}$ for $B=1\,$T.
L000238	
L000239	The metal sheet is modeled as single-layer graphene with linear dispersion
L000240	$\varepsilon_{\bm{k}} = \hbar v_F |\bm{k}|$ and Fermi velocity $v_F = 10^6\,$m/s. The
L000241	chemical potential is fixed at $\mu = 0.15\,$eV. The corresponding Fermi wavevector is
L000242	$k_F=2.28\times 10^8\,$m$^{-1}$, and the electron density which includes spin and valley
L000243	degeneracies is given by $n_s = k_F^2/\pi = 1.65\times 10^{16}\,$m$^{-2}$. Since the
L000244	chemical potential is much larger than the SPP energies considered, interband transitions
L000245	are negligible in the frequency range of interest. Consequently, the optical conductivity
L000246	is well described by the Drude form
L000247	$\sigma(\omega)= e_0^2 \mu /[\hbar \pi (2\eta -i\hbar\omega)]$.
L000248	
L000249	Before presenting the numerical results, we estimate the vacuum gap required for efficient
L000250	electron–photon coupling under energy and momentum conservation. Since the dominant
L000251	electronic states contributing to transport reside near the Fermi level, we take the
L000252	initial electron momentum as the Fermi momentum $k_F$. Absorption of a surface plasmon
L000253	with in-plane wavevector $q$ and energy $\hbar\omega$ imposes the condition
L000254	$q=\omega /v_F$. For SPP energy $\hbar\omega$ at $30\,$meV, the evanescent decay length in
L000255	vacuum is thus $l \sim 1/q \approx 22\,$nm. To ensure substantial photon tunneling across
L000256	the gap, the vacuum gap $d$ should be smaller than this length scale.
L000257	
L000258	\begin{figure}
L000259	\centering
L000260	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig2_new.pdf} \\
L000261	\caption{(a) Nonreciprocal photon flux factor $\Phi(q_x, \omega)$ plotted as a function of
L000262	  in-plane wavevector $q_x$ and photon energy $\hbar\omega$ for $q_y=0$ with magnetic
L000263	  field $B=4\,$T, electron damping $\eta =0.5\,$meV, and vacuum gap $d=2\,$nm.
L000264	  Photon absorption is strongly peaked along the dashed lines, which correspond to the
L000265	  single-particle excitations in graphene, given by $\omega = |q_x| v_F$ (dashed lines).
L000266	  (b) The effective drift velocity versus $\eta$. The temperatures of the magneto-optic
L000267	  medium and graphene are set to $T_2=400\,$K and $T_1=300\,$K, respectively. For visual
L000268	  clarity, the curve from Eq.~\eqref{Ie} is scaled by a factor of $10^{13}$.  }
L000269	\label{fig2}
L000270	\end{figure}
L000271	
L000272	In Fig.~\ref{fig2}(a), we show the nonreciprocal photon flux factor $\Phi(\bm{q},\omega)$
L000273	as a function of in-plane wavevector $q_x$ (with $q_y=0$) and SPP energy $\hbar\omega$
L000274	with magnetic field $B=4\,$T, electronic damping $\eta = 0.5\,$meV, and vacuum gap
L000275	$d=2\,$nm. The dashed lines correspond to the single-particle excitation condition in
L000276	graphene, $\omega = |q_x| v_F$, along which photon absorption is the strongest. From
L000277	Eq.~\eqref{L}, the dominant contribution to the electron transport comes from the region
L000278	in $(\bm{q}, \omega)$ space where the dispersion of the SPP intersects the single-particle
L000279	excitation spectrum. Because the electron spectrum is sharply peaked along $\omega =
L000280	|\bm{q}| v_F$, only those SPP modes that lie close to this line efficiently couple to the
L000281	electrons and contribute to current generation. Figure~\ref{fig2}(a) shows that the SPP
L000282	branch propagating in the $-x$ direction ($q_x<0$) possesses a larger spectral weight near
L000283	the single-particle excitation line than the branch propagating in the $+x$ direction
L000284	($q_x>0$). This difference originates from the nonreciprocal SPP shift, sketched in
L000285	Fig.~\ref{fig1}. As a result, plasmons with $q_x <0$ are absorbed more efficiently,
L000286	producing a net electron drift along the $-x$ direction.
L000287	
L000288	To have an intuitive measure, an effective drift velocity $v_d$ is introduced via
L000289	\begin{equation} \label{Ie_vd}

L000291	\end{equation}

L000293	$\eta$. The negative sign of $v_d$ confirms the electron flow direction inferred from
L000294	Fig.~\ref{fig2}(a).
L000295	The drift velocity magnitude decreases with increasing $\eta$ due to enhanced
L000296	momentum dissipation. The photon flux factor, governed by $|t_1^p|$, remains insensitive
L000297	to $\eta$ and thus does not counter this trend [See Fig.~\ref{fig3}(a)].
L000298	The drift velocity is small because only a narrow region of the plasmon spectrum satisfies
L000299	the kinematic matching for electronic transitions and contributes to the current.
L000300	The drift velocity is approximately $-0.05\,$pm/s for $\eta=0.1\,$meV. The
L000301	corresponding current density is approximately $0.14\,$fA/m.

L000313	We now provide numerical evidence demonstrating why a microscopic treatment is essential.
L000314	The total photon momentum flux transferred to the metal sheet can be written in a
L000315	Landauer-like form as~\cite{SM}
L000316	\begin{equation} \label{Px}
L000317	  P_x = \int_0^{\infty} \frac{d\omega}{2\pi} \int_{q>
L000318	  \omega/c}\frac{d^2\bm{q}}{(2\pi)^2} \hbar q_x \xi(\bm{q} ,\omega) N_{21}(\omega) ,
L000319	\end{equation}
L000320	with the photon transmission coefficient
L000321	\begin{equation}
L000322	  \xi(\bm{q},\omega) = \frac{4 \ {\rm Im}\big(r_2^p \big) {\rm Im}\big( r_1^p \big)
L000323	  e^{-2 |\gamma_0| d}}{|1 - r_1^p r_2^p e^{-2 |\gamma_0| d}|^2}.
L000324	\end{equation}
L000325	This expression has been employed to calculate the lateral force induced by the
L000326	nonreciprocal surface mode~\cite{lateral_17, lateral_21, GT24-2}; a microscopic derivation
L000327	is provided in the Supplemental Material~\cite{SM}.
L000328	Momentum conservation dictates that photons directly transfer momentum to the electrons.
L000329	This momentum is subsequently dissipated to the lattice through scattering, which
L000330	establishes the relaxation mechanism necessary for a steady electric current to develop.
L000331	Thus, we might employ the simple force-balance relation $P_x = m^* n_s v_d /\tau$ which
L000332	assumes a constant scattering time with $\tau =\hbar/(2\eta)$.
L000333	However, the momentum- and energy-conservation conditions shown in Eq.~\eqref{L} and
L000334	Fig.~\ref{fig2}(a) imply that only a narrow region of the plasmon spectrum satisfies the
L000335	kinematic matching for electronic transitions and thus contributes to the current. A
L000336	simple force-balance equation that ignores this selective coupling is therefore
L000337	inadequate.
L000338	
L000339	Moreover, the photon flux factor $\Phi$ entering Eq.~\eqref{Ie} and the
L000340	photon transmission coefficient $\xi$ in Eq.~\eqref{Px} have fundamentally different
L000341	physical meaning: $\Phi$ quantifies the flux of photons that can actually contribute to the
L000342	electronic transitions and drive an electron flow, while $\xi$ describes the photon
L000343	dissipation in the metal. This difference can also be reflected in the fact that, in the
L000344	limit of vanishing electronic damping ($\eta \rightarrow 0$), the
L000345	photon flux factor $\Phi$ remains finite, whereas the photon transmission coefficient
L000346	$\xi$ goes to zero [See Fig.~\ref{fig3}].
L000347	The electron-photon interaction, encoded in the Fock self-energy [see End Matter],
L000348	also renormalizes essential electronic parameters, including the scattering rate, the
L000349	carrier density, and the effective mass. Importantly, this self-energy depends on the
L000350	temperature profile and can vary over the energy range relevant to transport.
L000351	
L000352	For a quantitative comparison, the dashed curve in Fig.~\ref{fig2}(b) shows the drift
L000353	velocity obtained from the simple force-balance relation $P_x = m^* n_s v_d /\tau$
L000354	where the effective mass $m^*$ is taken as $m^* =\hbar k_F / v_F \approx 0.026m_e$
L000355	with $m_e$ the free-electron mass. The resulting values overestimate the microscopic
L000356	result by approximately $13$ orders of magnitude, demonstrating that a force-balance
L000357	picture fails utterly to describe the coupled electron-photon dynamics.
L000358	Moreover, the magnitude of the drift velocity calculated using this approch exhibits a
L000359	nonmonotonic dependence on the scattering rate $\eta$: it first increases and then
L000360	decreases. This is due to the competition between photon transmission and momentum
L000361	relaxation. At very small $\eta$, the photon transmission is low, which limits the photon
L000362	momentum flux $P_x$, as indicated by the behavior of ${\rm Im}(r_1^p)$ [See
L000363	Fig.~\ref{fig3}(b)].
L000364	As $\eta$ increases, $P_x$ initially rises. However, beyond a certain value, the explicit
L000365	$1/\eta$ factor representing increased momentum dissipation dominates and suppresses the
L000366	electron drift.
L000367	These drastic discrepancies underscore the necessity of a microscopic theory that properly
L000368	incorporates electron-photon interaction in transverse thermophotovoltaic effects.
L000369	
L000370	Photons that do not contribute to the current are absorbed via Drude absorption: the
L000371	oscillating electric field transfers energy to the electron gas by driving collective
L000372	oscillations. The excited electrons then relax through electron-phonon coupling,
L000373	converting energy to heat and transferring photon momentum to the lattice. This relaxation
L000374	process is characterized by $\eta$; indeed, both the radiative heat flux and total
L000375	photon momentum flux vanish as $\eta \rightarrow 0$. Crucially, this mechanical force
L000376	does not affect the current in Eq.~\eqref{Ie}, which describes electron motion relative to
L000377	the graphene lattice.
L000378	
L000379	{\it Discussion and conclusion.}
L000380	Regarding experimental feasibility, the predicted transverse current may be too small for
L000381	direct detection with current experimental technique. To raise the signal to a measurable
L000382	level, two principal routes can be pursued: enhancing the photon flux factor and
L000383	optimizing the electronic transition.
L000384	
L000385	By placing a second magneto-optic medium under identical magnetic field and temperature
L000386	conditions on the opposite side of the metal sheet, the resulting Fabry-Perot resonance
L000387	between the two media can substantially enhance the photon flux factor.
L000388	
L000389	A strategy to simultaneously realize both enhancements is to pattern periodic gratings on
L000390	the metal sheet. First, the grating periodicity folds the plasmon dispersion, opening
L000391	photonic band gaps that suppress SPP excitation for one propagation direction while
L000392	allowing it in the opposite direction, thereby increasing the momentum-transfer asymmetry.
L000393	Second, the grating grooves act as plasmonic resonators that trap and locally enhance the
L000394	electromagnetic field, increasing the photon flux factor. Through these two synergistic
L000395	mechanisms, the transverse electric current can be increased.
L000396	
L000397	An alternative approach is to replace the metal sheet with an intrinsic semiconductor or a
L000398	gated two-dimensional electron gas. The finite band gap (or the gate-tunable excitation
L000399	threshold) provides a sharp optical absorption edge. Because the nonreciprocal SPP
L000400	branches are shifted in frequency, one branch can lie above the absorption edge while the
L000401	other falls below it. Consequently, the semiconductor strongly absorbs SPPs propagating in
L000402	one direction while blocking those in the opposite direction, dramatically enhancing the
L000403	directional asymmetry of the photon-momentum transfer.
L000404	Thus, using a semiconductor as the current generator can alleviate heat dissipation by
L000405	improving thermoelectric conversion efficiency through relaxed kinematic matching.
L000406	This lifts the constraint present in metals where only a narrow intersection region
L000407	contributes and contributions from opposite propagation directions largely cancel.
L000408	
L000409	To assess the energy conversion efficiency and output power of this heat engine would
L000410	require attaching two metallic leads to the graphene sheet. Under operating conditions,
L000411	the induced voltage modifies the electronic states, making the local thermal equilibrium
L000412	assumption fail. Consequently, a framework that self-consistently accounts for the
L000413	nonequilibrium carrier distribution would be necessary.
L000414	The same nonequilibrium considerations apply to a signal-to-noise analysis, which would
L000415	require including electron-phonon scattering and other noise sources.
L000416	
L000417	The transverse thermophotovoltaic effect reported in this work differs from conventional
L000418	photon drag~\cite{photon_drag88, photon_drag19, photon_drag24, photon_drag25} in three
L000419	aspects: (i) the photons are thermal near-field photons with large in-plane momenta ($q\gg
L000420	\omega/c$), not coherent laser photons; (ii) the electric current is driven by a
L000421	temperature gradient, not an external optical beam; (iii) the directionality comes from
L000422	intrinsic SPP nonreciprocity, not sample asymmetry or oblique incidence.
L000423	
L000424	To conclude, we have demonstrated the generation of a transverse electric current driven
L000425	by near-field thermal radiation via nonreciprocal surface plasmon polaritons, based on a
L000426	microscopic theory that accounts for electron-photon interactions.
L000427	
L000428	
L000429	The derived electric current expression, Eq.~\eqref{Ie}, inherently incorporates kinematic
L000430	matching and momentum-resolved photon flux, providing a rigorous theoretical foundation
L000431	for this phenomena. This work establishes a design principle to harness the nonreciprocal
L000432	surface modes for ``transverse thermophotovoltaics" with potential applications in
L000433	nanoscale energy conversion and active radiative thermal management.

L000457	The total Hamiltonian of the system is partitioned as
L000458	\begin{equation}
L000459	  H_{\rm tot} = H_{\rm ph} + H_1 + H_{1, \rm ph} .
L000460	\end{equation}
L000461	We adopt the temporal gauge by setting the scalar potential to zero so that the
L000462	electromagnetic Hamiltonian is expressed in terms of the vector potential $\bm{A}$
L000463	as~\cite{QFT-Fradkin, Lifshitz_book, JSW23}
L000464	\begin{equation} \label{H_ph}
L000465	  H_{\rm ph} = \frac{1}{2} \int d^3\bm{r} \left[ \epsilon_0 \epsilon_r \big(
L000466	  \partial_t \bm{A} \big)^2 + \mu_0^{-1} \big( \nabla \times \bm{A} \big)^2 \right] ,
L000467	\end{equation}
L000468	with $\epsilon_0$ and $\mu_0$ the vacuum permittivity and permeability. The
L000469	space-dependent relative permittivity is $\epsilon_r = \epsilon_{\rm MO}$ for $z<0$
L000470	which is filled with magneto-optic medium and $\epsilon_r = 1$ for $z>0$.
L000471	The two-dimensional metal sheet is described using a tight-binding model with
L000472	\begin{equation}
L000473	  H_1 = \sum_{i, j} c_i^\dag H_{ij} c_j ,
L000474	\end{equation}
L000475	where $i$ and $j$ label the electron sites at positions $\bm{r}_i$ and $\bm{r}_j$.
L000476	The electron-photon interaction for the metal sheet is considered in $H_{1, \rm ph}$.
L000477	Gauge invariance is ensured by the Peierls substitution, which couples the electrons to
L000478	the photonic field with~\cite{JSW23}
L000479	\begin{equation} \label{Peierls}
L000480	  H_1 + H_{1, \rm ph} = \sum_{i, j} c_i^\dag  H_{ij} c_j
L000481	  \exp\left[ \frac{e_0}{i\hbar} \int_{\bm{r}_j}^{{\bm{r}_i}} d\bm{r} \cdot \bm{A}(\bm{r})
L000482	  \right] .
L000483	\end{equation}
L000484	To get the explicit interaction Hamiltonian, the line integral is approximated with the
L000485	trapezoidal rule
L000486	\begin{equation}
L000487	  \int_{\bm{r}_j}^{{\bm{r}_i}} d\bm{r} \cdot \bm{A}(\bm{r})
L000488	  \approx \frac{1}{2} (\bm{A}_i + \bm{A}_j) \cdot (\bm{r}_i - \bm{r}_j) ,
L000489	\end{equation}
L000490	with the notation $\bm{A}_i \equiv \bm{A}(\bm{r}_i)$.
L000491	Performing Taylor expansion to the exponential in Eq.~\eqref{Peierls} up to the second
L000492	order in the lattice constant, the interaction Hamiltonian is written as
L000493	\begin{equation} \label{H_int}
L000494	  H_{1,\rm ph} = H_{\rm para} + H_{\rm dia} ,
L000495	\end{equation}
L000496	which consists of paramagnetic and diamagnetic contributions.
L000497	The paramagnetic contribution is given explicitly in real space as~\cite{JSW23}
L000498	\begin{equation}
L000499	  H_{\rm para} = \frac{e_0}{2} \sum_{i,j, l,\mu} c_i^\dag v_{ij}^\mu (\delta_{il} +
L000500	  \delta_{jl}) A_{l \mu} c_j ,
L000501	\end{equation}
L000502	where the indices $i$, $j$, and $l$ denote the electron sites, and $\mu =x,y$ labels the
L000503	Cartesian directions. Transforming to the wavevector representation, the electronic
L000504	Hamiltonian becomes
L000505	\begin{equation}
L000506	  H_1 = \sum_{\bm{k}} \varepsilon_{\bm{k}} c_{\bm{k}}^{\dag}c_{\bm{k}} ,
L000507	\end{equation}
L000508	where $\varepsilon_{\bm{k}}$ is the band dispersion. The paramagnetic interaction is expressed
L000509	as
L000510	\begin{equation}
L000511	  H_{\rm para} = -e_0 \sum_{\bm{q}, \bm{k}} \bm{v}(\bm{k},\bm{q}) \cdot \bm{A}(\bm{q})
L000512	  c_{\bm{k}+\bm{q}}^{\dag}c_{\bm{k}} ,
L000513	\end{equation}
L000514	with the symmetrized velocity vertex as
L000515	\begin{equation}
L000516	  \bm{v}(\bm{k},\bm{q}) = \big[ \bm{v}(\bm{k}) + \bm{v}(\bm{k} + \bm{q}) \big] / 2 .
L000517	\end{equation}

L000519	In the absence of the electron-photon interaction, the non-interacting retarded and
L000520	advanced electronic Green's functions are given by
L000521	\begin{equation}
